utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I see one additional member on the team, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Counsel. We are joined today by Mr. Thomas Hannis, who will be leading the first witness in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for introducing Mr. Hannis, Mr. Harmon. Before I give you the opportunity to proceed with your open statement, I'd like to announce that the Chamber allows Mr. Krajisnik to make a short statement after the opening statement of the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honours, Counsel. Yesterday, when I concluded the day, I was discussing criminal responsibility under Article 7(3), and I had focussed my attention on one part of the third element, that is, whether or not the accused had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit crimes or had done so. I would now like to focus on the other part of that element, whether the accused had actual knowledge that his subordinates were about to commit crimes or had done so. Now, actual knowledge can be established either through direct evidence or through circumstantial evidence, from which it can be inferred that the accused had actual knowledge. We intend, in the course of this trial, to present both types of evidence to establish this particular element. The commission of experts set forth in their final report a number of relevant factors that can be considered when focussing on the circumstantial evidence of knowledge, and I will identify some of those factors now, starting with the number of illegal acts that occurred; the type of illegal acts; the scope of the illegal acts; the time during which the illegal acts occurred; the number and types of troops involved; the geographical location of the acts; the widespread occurrence of the acts; the modus operandi of similar illegal acts; and the officers and the staff involved. Now, our evidence will show that the accused had direct knowledge, both that crimes were about to be committed and that they had been committed. Our evidence will show that throughout the war, the Bosnian Serb army and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the police, informed the presidency on a daily basis about the events on the ground. The presidency received regular reports through the government, which was in regular contact with the municipalities, with the crisis staffs, with the Serb Autonomous Regions, and it also received reports from the individual ministries. In addition, General Ratko Mladic reported personally and frequently to the presidency. He reported about the events that were occurring on the ground. Now, according to a document that we will present to Your Honours during this trial -- this document is entitled "The analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the VRS in 1992". It describes a communication system that was fully functional. I will quote part of that report, and I quote: "With a high degree of certainty, we can say that the existing communication system meets the needs of command coordination and report needs at all levels, from the supreme command, the supreme commander, the General Staff, to lower levels." Our evidence will show that the crimes that form part of this indictment were reported directly to the Main Staff of the VRS and to the presidency, and that the presidency was informed on a daily basis about events and problems that took place on the ground. Let me again take Your Honours back to the 34th Bosnian Serb Assembly session and quote for you the words of General Milan Gvero, who said, and I quote: "The Main Staff has consistently provided oral and written information to the commander-in-chief, the prime minister, the Minister of Defence, and others, about all the problems." Now, let me give you some examples of the types of evidence of those problems that we will present to Your Honours, and these are taken from the reports of the VRS Main Staff. One is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps, dated the 22nd of August, 1992. It is a regular combat report, and I quote from it: "A massacre against civilians, Muslim men, was committed on 21 August, between 1830 and 1900 hours. It was committed by a group of policemen escorting a convoy of refugees to Travnik. The massacre took place at Koricanske Stijene, in the canyon of Ilomska River at Mount Vlasic. About 100 people were killed in various ways and left in the canyon." Now, this particular crime is identified in schedule B of our indictment, at point 15.5, and this particular report, which went to the Main Staff, was reported at a time when the accused was a member of the expanded presidency. Let me turn to another report, again from the 1st Krajina Corps, issued to the VRS Main Staff. It is dated the 4th of November, 1992. It also reports a crime. And let me quote from that report: "In the area of Kotor Varos," and, Your Honours, Kotor Varos is one of the municipalities identified in our indictment. It goes on to say: "About 40 Green Beret members were killed and about 200 captured. A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade." And the report goes on. Now, this particular event, this crime, is identified in schedule B at point 11. And again, our evidence will show when this particular crime was reported to the VRS Main Staff, the accused was a member of the expanded presidency. Now, Your Honours, our evidence will show that the plight of the victims of this ethnic cleansing campaign were daily fare in the media, to which the Bosnian Serb leadership had access. And I recall quite well, and Your Honours may recall as well, that the brutality of this campaign was depicted in daily fare in the media. And I will turn once again to an exhibit that I have previously shown you. This exhibit from Bijeljina. There will be many more pictures from the media that were depicted in 1992, but this image in particular is one which shocked the world and one that was in the media and caused the international community such concern that they made a series of reports and took a series of official actions to indeed -- that resulted finally in this creation of this institution. But this is the type of image that was in the media. Other sorts of haunting images as well appeared daily in the media. This, for example, is the type of an image that -- one of many that was shown in the media, depicting the conditions in the Bosnian Serb camps, camps that were created by the Bosnian Serbs, that were instrumental in the ethnic cleansing campaign. These images -- and if we could have the next image now on the screen. The next image also is an image that was in the media. It shows a scene, the conditions how a number of Bosnian Muslim civilians were detained in the Manjaca camp. There are other images as well that would put the accused on notice. Let me turn to the next image, a typical image that we saw daily in the newspapers, showing the plight of refugees who were being forced from their homes. Other images would have put the accused on notice. Let me turn to another image, showing what was part of the heritage - can I have the next image, please? - part of the heritage of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. humanity. This is a picture of a mosque, the Alidza mosque, built in the middle of the 1500s that truly was a magnificent sight. This next image is part of its interior. And what images we saw of those sites that had been part of our common heritage, we saw the following types of images. If I could have the next image. This is what's left of the Alidza mosque, and we saw repeatedly in the course of 1992 similar types of images where this common heritage had been reduced to piles of stone and rubble, where these beautiful structures had become parking lots or vacant lots. Now, Your Honours, the evidence will show that the crimes that were being committed by the Bosnian Serb forces against the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were widely reported, and complaints about them were made directly to the accused, to Radovan Karadzic, and to other Bosnian Serb and Serbian leaders, by diplomats, by journalists, by non-governmental organisations such as UNHCR, or the Red Cross, or Amnesty International. Our evidence will show that the Bosnian Serb leadership was receiving this type of information, and I will refer you to a piece of evidence, one of many that we will present during the course of this trial, the minutes of the 5th session of the presidency, dated the 10th of June, 1992, at a time when Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the presidency. And in those minutes, it reflects that the presidency received information in the form of reports from the international community. Now, examples of such reports from the international community will be led in evidence and presented in evidence by us. I'd like to refer to two specific reports. Those reports were prepared by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, who was a Special Rapporteur of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights. Both of those reports were issued at a time when the accused was a member of the expanded presidency. One report is dated the 28th of August, 1992, and the other report was issued on the 27th of October, 1992. In the 27 October report, Mr. Mazowiecki said, and I quote: "As indicated in the first report, the Muslim population are the principal victims and are virtually threatened with extermination." Now, Mr. Mazowiecki's report, which was prepared over 11 years ago, described ethnic cleansing with striking accuracy. What his report said was as follows: "Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather its goal." Now, a veritable flood of credible information about the crimes that were being committed by the Bosnian Serb forces inundated the Bosnian Serb leadership. According to the evidence that we will present, their responses to these reports yielded little other than denials that such crimes had occurred, surprise that such crimes had occurred, complaints that the other side was doing the same thing. Sometimes it resulted in directives issued to their forces to comply with international humanitarian law, but seldom were those directives enforced. Now, the last element that we must establish to establish criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) is that the accused failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the offences from occurring or to punish the perpetrators. As the person who sat at the pinnacle of power within the Bosnian Serb leadership, Momcilo Krajisnik had fulsome de jure and de facto authority to prevent perpetrators from committing crimes or to punish them for having done so. As the supreme commander of the army, the members of the presidency, including Mr. Krajisnik, had the duty and the power under the constitution and existing laws to order the army and to order the police to investigate crimes, and they actually exercised that power. I will not go into the details of those legal authorities. I'll leave that for expert witnesses to testify about. But I'd like to provide you with some examples to illustrate the fact that the presidency did indeed have the power to investigate crimes, and these examples are taken directly from the minutes of the presidency meetings where Mr. Krajisnik was present. We will introduce these minutes as evidence in this case. At the 14th session of the presidency, which was on the 3rd of July, 1992, the presidency ordered the police to investigate the activity of paramilitary units in the municipalities of Gacko and Nevesinje, for terrorist acts directed against the civilian population. At the 24th session of the presidency, the 6th of August, 1992, the minister of the interior was ordered to investigate the behaviour of all civilian authorities and individuals guarding prisoners of war, and that information was supposed to be passed back to the presidency. At that very same session, the presidency ordered that a commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people be established, not a commission to investigate war crimes against all people, but against Serbian people. And finally, Your Honours, another example: On the 26th of October, 1992, the presidency ordered the military authority and the command, the VRS command, to investigate accusations that had been made in respect of a politician by the name of Branko Simic. Now, in addition to the powers that the presidency had to investigate, they had other authorities and other powers at their disposal that would have deterred and would have prevented the systematic commission of crimes throughout the territory which they occupied. Our evidence will show that they had the power to directly affect the judicial system. They had the power to make judicial appointments, including the appointments of prosecutors, deputy prosecutors and secretaries to the military disciplinary courts. They had the power to adopt regulations on military discipline; the power to reduce, ameliorate, or rescind any disciplinary measure or punishment. They actually had the power to prescribe disciplinary measures or punishments, and they could decide a variety of personnel matters, such as promotions of officers, appointments of officers, transfer of officers; and they could decide as well on the admission to active military service, or the cessation of active military service of general officers. Our evidence will show that the presidency appointed military judges and prosecutors who would look the other way when the victims of crimes were non-Serbs. They appointed civilian judges and prosecutors who never prosecuted members of the police for crimes that the police had committed. We will call witnesses, and we will introduce evidence of actual court records that demonstrate how the court systems actually operated in 1992. What is glaringly obvious from these records is that Bosnian Serb perpetrators were seldomly, if ever, prosecuted and punished where the victims were non-Serbs. There were rare and exceptional cases when it did happen, but it was quite common in those cases for the perpetrators to be released back to their military units for active service. However, where the evidence shows that the victim was a Serb, the records demonstrate a different approach, and in those cases, the records will demonstrate that the prosecutions did indeed proceed, there were convictions, and punishment was meted out. Finally, our evidence will show that the pattern of selective prosecution made deterrence of ethnically directed crimes impossible, and indeed, it encouraged the perpetrators to commit additional crimes with impunity. Your Honours, this concludes my opening remarks. I thank you for your patience. We will undertake to present the evidence in this case as expeditiously as possible, while at the same time bearing in mind the solemn responsibilities imposed upon us by the international community. We are satisfied that at the end of the case, after your having heard all of the evidence, you will find Momcilo Krajisnik guilty of the charges in the indictment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. The list the Prosecution would provide is already provided or will be provided? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibits that I have used are here on this trolley, and I'm prepared to hand them up now, if Your Honours would like. Or I can do it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that they will be tendered into evidence at a later stage of the proceedings. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, we would like to have an overview on what actually has been presented during the opening statement so that we're fully informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution has now concluded its opening statement, and upon your request, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber allows you to make a statement, a statement on which, in accordance with Rule 84 bis, you're not required to make a solemn declaration, on which statement you'll not be examined by the parties. I also inform you that Rule 84 bis, under (B) reads: The Trial Chamber shall decide on the probative value, if any, of the statements." So whatever you say in your statement, the Chamber could attribute probative value to that, if it decides so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I would like to thank you for allowing me to speak briefly at the beginning of my trial. What I wish to say is that I have carefully listened, yesterday and today, to the Prosecutor's opening address, and the charges are very serious that are put forth by the Prosecution. I would like to assure you that everything charged against me is not true. I am innocent on all counts of the indictment. I am not guilty. And that is why I hope and believe that in the course of this trial, you, Your Honours, will have enough relevant and truthful documents and evidence to be convinced that I'm not guilty and that the indictment is probably addressed to the wrong person. The Prosecutor also states that they will prove the indictment, and I believe and hope that there will be no documents here that are not true, based on which they will try to do that, and I'm convinced that they will not succeed in proving the charges. Finally, I would like to also state, without abusing your goodwill in permitting me to speak, I would like to state that I believe in God and in justice. I believe that truth will win and that, after having spent some years in prison, I will finally be a free man. I would like to ask you to make sure that the truth wins, since yesterday and today I'm living for that day. I would like the truth to win. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Let me assure you that the Trial Chamber will do whatever is in its ability to find the truth. This brings us to the next stage of this trial, that is, the presentation of Prosecution evidence, and Mr. Hannis, because I understand that I have to address you, would you please call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger will be excused, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our first witness will be Isak Gasi.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a witness statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the interpreters are asking for a copy of the witness statement, if available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm told that we anticipated there would be a break between the statements and the first witness, and we are in the process of getting those materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps even without a break, you could take care that the material will arrive as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Welcome in this courtroom. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, and I see that the text has already been handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gasi as I understand. Mr. Gasi you'll first be examined by the Prosecution, so please listen carefully and please answer the questions put to you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Isak Gasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, 1957, in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where is Brcko located?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Brcko is located in the north-eastern part of Bosnia. It is on the River Sava, which separates us from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I just interrupt you for one second? The witness has asked just before entering the courtroom to deliver some paperwork to the Prosecution. We are not aware of what it is, Mr. Gasi. Could it suffer some delay, so that you'll first be examined, or is it necessary to deliver that right away? It's a bit uncommon to give documents at the very start of your examination to the Prosecution, but I want to have this as transparent as possible, that since you asked for it and since we have not done it yet, that you're aware of that. Unless there's a specific reason you could give us why it should be delivered to the Prosecution at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I address that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just before we started, Mr. Gasi was looking at a copy of a map that was one of the exhibits on the list we propose to show him and he was making some marks on that map to indicate locations that he'll be talking about, and he brought that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, would there be any problem if I look at it before giving it to the Prosecution, so that I'm aware and that I can verify that this is the contents of the document? And is there any observation to be made from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No observation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Would you allow me just to have a look at it to see that that is it and then give it to the Prosecution? I see you're nodding yes, but for the transcript, it's unclear. If you just nod, it will not be on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a map of the town of Brcko. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks from a distance as a map and some explanatory marks made on it. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we could show Exhibit 39.023 on our list to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise what that is? Would you please tell the Court what that is.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. That is the municipality of Brcko and the town of Brcko on a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gasi, can you tell us where -- did you spend your whole life in Brcko up until the time of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, all my life, up to the beginning of war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: For 15 years I worked as a controller and the person in charge of the maintenance of electrical devices in Brcko. From 1979 to 1992. All in all, about 15 years all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you do any national military service during that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. In 1977, I did my compulsory service, according to the law, and I spent about 14 or 15 months in the army. I did that like every other able-bodied man at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of duties did you perform in the army? What unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I was in a traffic unit. I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to your military service and your work with the electrical company, did you engage in any other kind of activity in Yugoslavia for which you gained some local fame, if I can say that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: When I was 12 or 13, I started rowing in a kayak club in Brcko. So from the age of am 12 or 13, I've been engaged in rowing, to this very day. And I was quite well known in my own town and in the former Yugoslavia, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you compete in that sport at a national and international level?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I represented Yugoslavia, both as a junior and then as a senior. I participated in world championships and international regattas all over Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what the ethnic make-up of Brcko was before the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: According to the census which took place on the eve of the war, there were about 44 to 45 per cent Muslims, as they were called at the time. Today they're called Bosniaks. The second-ranking people were Serbs, accounting for 22 per cent in Brcko municipality; and some 17 to 20 per cent were Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before 1990, did there come a time where the political situation in the former Yugoslavia changed?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As far as I followed the media, the newspapers and the TV, there were first some conflicts in Slovenia, and later on those moved to Croatia. And then people started rallying on an ethnic basis. And that's how it all started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the former Yugoslavian leader Tito died, were there a change in the political system?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, there was a change. The last communist league congress took place in Belgrade. I don't know exactly when. After Tito died, the situation was stable for some five or six years, and then things started happening in Kosovo. The last party congress which took place in Belgrade, I believe that it was in May 1990, I believe that the League of Communists was dissolved there and people started establishing new political parties in Slovenia, in Croatia, and finally in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Divisions started and ethnically based parties started gathering people around themselves. And that's all I could learn from the TV and the newspapers which were printed at the time. When the League of Communists broke up, new nationalist parties were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir. Can you tell me: The three primary parties, based on the three ethnic groups you told us existed in Brcko, what were they?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There was the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, which was primarily a Muslim party; then there was the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. That was the party of Bosniak Croats. And there was the SDS, which rallied around itself members of the Serbian people, the Serbian Democratic Party, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And sir, I'm sorry. I didn't ask you before. Could you tell the Court your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This is something I don't volunteer, but let me tell you: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your father's ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He is an Albanian from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you present in Brcko and aware of the pre-election activities before the multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the organisation or committee. They asked me to join them as the SDA was being set up. I told them I would do it, on a condition that this work was public and that my appearances were not political ones. Apart from that, I would appear in every of their rallies that were open to public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did all three of the parties hold various rallies before the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you eventually become a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I became a member of the SDA. I participated at their founding congress in Sarajevo, in May 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I remained a member up to the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then I publicly said that I no longer wished to be a member of any political party; I wanted to be on my own, my own free agent. And that's what I am to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time, did you personally make any public appearances on TV and speak about political matters?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't speak about any political matters. On one occasion before the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had an opportunity to give an interview, a very short interview, about the Bosnia and Herzegovina I thought I could live in. It was a short interview, in which I said that we all had to endeavour to live in one single state, whose name would be Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that we should all live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the results of the multi-party elections in 1990 in Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: According to what I know, I believe that the SDP, the former communists, the Socialist Democratic Party, won the majority of the votes. They were followed by the SDA and then the HDZ, and if I'm not mistaken, the third was the Serbian Democratic Party, and a small percentage was won by some other parties which were multi-ethnic, of mixed ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a result of those elections, did the nationalist parties do anything to try and avoid the communists from retaining control?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They set up a coalition, according to the law which was then in effect, they set up a coalition to push out communists. They wanted to prevent the communists from gaining any seats in the municipal parliament. That's why they set up the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there some sort of agreement among the three nationalist parties to share that power and appoint positions among themselves?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who became the president of the Municipal Assembly as a result in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Mustafa Ramic, a member of the SDA, was the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who or from which party the head of the Executive Board of the Assembly was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He was from the Serbian Democratic Party. His name was Petar or Pero Markovic. In any case, his family name was Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who or which candidate was selected to be the police chief?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Stjepan Filipovic, from the Croatian Democratic Union, was the head of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the commander or the head of the local TO, Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Major Milisav Milutinovic. I don't know whether he was a member of the SDS or not, but in any event, his ethnic origin was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who some of the other local SDS leaders were in Brcko at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The president of the Serbian Democratic Party for the town of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brcko was Milenko Vojinovic, also known as Beli. The vice-president or one of the vice-presidents was Bosko Maricic, another one was Djordje Ristanic. I knew some other people. One of them worked with me. He was a member of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I knew quite a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you mentioned earlier that a conflict had begun to occur in Slovenia and Croatia. As a result of that, was there a mobilisation of young men of military age in Bosnia, and in particular, in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. People received call-up papers, and they were required to go to their assigned units, which were actually reserve units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that call-up began?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date or month. It all coincided with the events in Slovenia. Actually, a few months later, people started receiving those call-up papers, and they were asked to report to their war units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Brcko municipality, was there any difference in the nature of the response to the military call-up between the three different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: At the beginning, all the three ethnic groups received call-up papers, but they did not respond to them to the same extent. Later on, things changed. Some people decided to abandon the army. They went home and they said they didn't want to participate in all that. Even many Serbs started abandoning those units which were stationed in the local garrison in Brcko. That was just their way to show that they didn't want to participate in any of that. In any event, the majority of people who stayed in those units were the local Serbs from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, as a result of your work with the electric company, was your job such that you were able to travel around the municipality frequently?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: If not every day, then every other day I was moving around. I was in charge of the maintenance and control of measuring devices. So I would travel all over the municipality of Brcko at that time. I would go to all the villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your travels in late 1991 or early 1992, did you see any signs that indicated the existence of something called an SAO, or a Serb Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. At the exit of the town of Brcko, towards Bijeljina, there was a board resembling a traffic sign, with the inscription "SAO Semberija and Majevica." And if you went to the eastern side of Brcko, there was also a board with the inscription "SAO Serbian Krajina." There was nothing in the very town, but the moment you left the town, some 10 kilometres around the town there were boards. And that was, I believe, already at the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you first saw this sign, did you know what that was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As I've already said, there was an abbreviation. However, people talked. There were stories around the town. There were rumours. And later on, we realised what the SAO stood for, SAO Krajina or SAO Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you learn that it stood for, and what was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: SAO meant the Serbian Autonomous Region and meant a division into ethnic parts. I never saw anything like that before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the referendum in February of 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I took part in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what the question was that was presented in the referendum, what that vote was about?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I think that the question was taken from the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the existing Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the sense of it was: Are you for an independent sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, a union of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats? So it was something to that effect, yes or no, and then you would choose your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there political rallies held in Brcko municipality shortly before the referendum about that issue?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, there were political rallies, gatherings of people. And I say again it was ethnically based. Some were for, some were against, others were not in favour. Yes, there were all three ethnic groups gathered for these rallies. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to attend a rally held for Serbs regarding the referendum before that vote in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There was one rally -- actually, it was the Serbian Democratic Party organised a cultural society. It was called Prosvjeta, enlightenment, and this rally took place in the cultural hall in Brcko. All from the Serbian Democratic Party from Sarajevo appeared at this rally, except, I think, for Mr. Karadzic. He wasn't there. Everybody else, including Mr. Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, Aleksa Buha, Nikola Koljevic, were there. On that occasion, there was also another gentleman from the Republic of Serbia who was introduced at the rally as the minister for the Serbs across the Drina River. There were also a couple of authors, writers, from Belgrade, and I think also two members of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally attend this rally?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what the speeches were about, what the message was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In the beginning, when the rally began, they were going to talk about the cultural and artistic heritage of the Serbian people. But as the rally went on and different speakers appeared, this turned actually into a political rally, where I did not feel very comfortable. People were jumping up, shouting out threats; others would get up to calm them down. There was a lot of political tension there. So if you happened to be from a different ethnic group or of a different religion, it would have been better for you to leave that hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned threats. What kind of threats?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I remember a couple of the speakers. Amongst them, I remember a speech by this minister from the Republic of Serbia. At the beginning of his speech, he said that the Serbian people should live together with others, and by the end of the speech he said that nobody had the right to separate the Serbian people from Serbia, nobody had the right to speak on behalf of the Serbian people, the Serbian people, if they don't get what they're asking for in Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina can always count on Serbia, they can receive all kinds of assistance from Serbia. So that's how it went. That's the sense of it. After this speaker, the academicians also talked. They talked about the wars that the Serbian people waged throughout history, the blood that was spilled by the Serbian people for freedom. If it could not be done in this way, then it will be done by war. So that's how it proceeded, and eventually the atmosphere became very tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you to another topic, Mr. Gasi. In 1991, could you tell us and tell the Judges where you were living in Brcko, what part of town.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It's near the centre of the town. My building is near the JNA garrison in Brcko. It's perhaps about 50 metres away. My balcony is about 50 metres away from the JNA facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you live in a house or an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It's an apartment building, a flat in an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What floor did you live on?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see into the actual facility of the JNA from your apartment? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I could see the entire garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other JNA facilities or garrisons in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a facility where they had the garages for the heavy vehicles, tanks, and trucks. There was also a military facility, as well as a warehouse of ammunitions and explosives, on the road from Brcko to Loncari, near the village of Krepsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Apart from the garage for the vehicles and the warehouse for the ammunition and explosives, were there any other facilities other than the garrison next to your apartment, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Near my apartment, there was only the garrison. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on observations from your apartment and from your travels related to your work, in 1991 did you have occasion to see whether the JNA was involved in providing arms to any of the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were always people in the barracks who were in uniforms of the JNA. However, when I was going through the villages around villages near Brcko, I was present when these people were distributing weapons to the local population from those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And which population or which villages are you talking about receiving the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They are villages which had 100 per cent Serb population. Serbian Brezovo Polje, Bukvica, Korenica, Potocari, Gredice, Sandici, Trnjaci, Mutica, Pukis, Bobetino Brdo. All of these villages were in the municipality of Brcko, or they belonged to Ugljevik or Bijeljina. But all of them were within a radius of 30 or 40 kilometres south-east of Brcko. And from 1990 to 1992, in April, I went to all of those villages. Perhaps not every day, but every other day. I passed through them very often. I would sit down and talk to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see weapons being provided by the JNA to any of the Croat or Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anyone else participating with the JNA in the distribution of weapons to the Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: From what I saw at that time, somebody would be in front of the local community centre in that village. They would be standing there. In Serbian Gredica on one occasion I saw a TAM 5.000 500-D trucks when it brought these boxes with automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and people were waiting in front of the local community centre building. They said weapons will be distributed. The truck came. So I was there for about an hour, and I watched as the weapons were being distributed. And this was noted down. In the JNA, each rifle has its own booklet. So if you receive this weapon, you have to sign the book, and it says that such-and-such a person received this rifle, and it also states how many bullets you were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Within the town of Brcko itself did you see any of this arming activity of Serbs going on?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: One of my neighbours - this is an example - was always dressed in a camouflage JNA uniform. He would go to town or he would go to cafes in Brcko. They even brought automatic rifles into the cafes, and you could see hand grenades hanging from their belts. They didn't abuse anyone. They didn't touch anyone. But it wasn't pleasant to sit with people who had two belts with bullets around them. So times had changed. It wasn't the way I remembered the JNA. It wasn't like that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During 1991, from your apartment next to the JNA garrison, did you notice any changes in the nature or level of activity at the JNA garrison in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were changes. Before, every morning I had the opportunity to hear the bugle and the wake-up call and the young conscripts who would appear in front of the buildings of the garrison. However, in the course of 1991, this stopped, and suddenly mature people began appearing, in their 40s. There were no longer any of these young men around. And for the first time, I saw men wearing the SMB camouflage uniforms with red berets on their heads, which, as far as I remember, I never saw when I was in the army. This is something that I recall. On a couple of occasions when my wife and I took walks by the garrison, I saw those people in red berets, training some local men, local Serbs from my town, training them to place police handcuffs on, taking their pistols out and pointing them at one another. All of this went out right along the fence which divides the garrison from the street on which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These older soldiers with red berets, did you recognise them? Were they local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Some of them were. The others, I didn't know. From my neighbourhood, actually, from my building there were three such men. Amongst them was Ranko Cesic. Also two brothers who lived in the same entrance that I lived in and there was another neighbour from the middle entrance. He was also wearing a uniform and one of these red berets on his head. They even used to come home wearing those same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I want to ask you about some of the political activity that was going on in Brcko town in early 1992. Were you aware of the events that were happening with the local Municipal Assembly and discussions about the future of Brcko town?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I attended the assembly session of the Brcko town on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were some of the proceedings televised as well of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Local Brcko television broadcast parts of those meetings, and I had the opportunity, with a friend of mine who was a journalist, to attend this meeting. There were many other people who observed the meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what in particular do you remember about this meeting you're describing? Do you recall approximately when it was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date, but I think it was in mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened at this meeting? What was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: A couple of people who joined the discussion said: We don't want the town to be divided. Those who would like to divide it can do so, but they can do so without us. People also shouted this out from their seats. At one point, Djordje Ristanic got up and he slammed his fist on the table: "We will divide it or we will have problems." And he said that the last deadline was the 4th of May, but he didn't actually say what would happen after the 4th of May. It was just it has to be divided or there will be all sorts of things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, who was Djordje Ristanic? What party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He was from the Serbian Democratic Party, and he was one of the vice-presidents of the SDS. He was in the Executive Board of the SDS, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this meeting, do you recall if he was -- what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He wasn't the only one who was wearing the reserves uniform of the JNA. There was also Mr. Millisa Milutinovic and some other gentlemen from the SDS who were there. And they were all wearing JNA uniforms. I think Ristanic was just a captain by rank. I think that he was, unless the insignia had changed at the time without me knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Dr. Beli, Milenko Vojinovic, was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, he was there also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what his position was in the SDS or the government?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDS of the town board. I'm not sure whether he was a member of the assembly of Brcko, though. I don't think that he was a member of the Municipal Assembly. I think he was there in the capacity of an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what this discussion about the division was? What was supposed to be done? How was a division supposed to occur?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: After this rally, and even before, photocopies began to appear Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around town, depicting the inner part of town. And what I saw on these maps, and also from what I heard, the Serbs were asking for the south-eastern part of the town and a larger part of the centre of town, which, by my estimate, would constitute about two-thirds of it. Mainly, they were asking for the industrial zone and a larger part of the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was a physical separation with the different ethnic groups living in different parts of town?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The line -- there was probably a physical line. The fact that I remained on the other side of that line. I don't know what else it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this time, how were the people living in Brcko? Did each group live in a separate part of town or were they intermixed?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: We were always intermixed. This line of separation would actually divide many families. Some would remain on one side, and the others on the other side. So I don't know what to tell you to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you know, sir: In Brcko town itself, what were the relative proportions of the three ethnic groups? Which one had the most and which had the least?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The most numerous were Muslims in the town itself, and then there were Serbs, and then Croats, to a somewhat lesser percentage. But from what I know, I think that the Serbs did not constitute a majority in any of the local communities except for Grcica and Potocari. These are the town local communes. But in the other communes, I think that most probably the Muslims constituted the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe you said that meeting was in about mid-April. I want to take you to the end of April 1992. Did anything unusual happen in Brcko town on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning of the 30th of April - it was 4.30 in the morning, to be precise - I was woken up by two powerful explosions. I have a wife and a child, so we got up. One window was broken on my building, actually, in my apartment, and then a couple of other windows were also broken on the other side. In the beginning, we didn't know what had caused the explosion, but later the telephones were working. We called one another, and later on we found out that two bridges were blown up across the Sava River. One of them was a railway bridge and the other was a bridge for regular passenger and vehicle traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall about what time of day this was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you this was in the morning, at 4.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the River Sava, what was on the other side of the River Sava from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other bridges in Brcko besides the railway bridge and the other bridge you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were two other bridges, but they go across the Brka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd like to show the witness a photograph, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. May we show the witness Exhibit 38.061.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I do understand that finally the Registry would like to give the final numbers to the exhibit. So Madam Registrar will then give the number by putting to you what number it finally will be. Madam Registrar, this will be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map of BiH with Brcko highlighted, bearing ERN number 04021847 will be Prosecution Exhibit number P1. And the next exhibit to be tendered will be Prosecution Exhibit number P2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you have a photo on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you recognise that, tell the Judges what that is.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This is the bridge over the Sava River, in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that picture depict the portion of the bridge that had fallen in the river as a result of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I was here, at that place where that section is missing, on that day. Yes, that is that section of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that how it looked that day when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Exactly like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Back up a second. After you heard the explosion, did you go to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't go there. I got up, and then at about 6.30 I had to go to work, because I have to go to work at 7.00 every morning. So I started walking from my house to the electric company, and when I got there to the Elektrodistribucija, our director said we could return home. So I returned home and then I told my wife I'm going to see the bridge over the Sava, because I knew that people were talking that it had been blown up. So it was maybe about 9.30 when I came to look at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got down by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In the very centre of town, just before the police station, I saw a couple of human corpses on the sidewalk. There's a small park just opposite from the SUP building, actually, and somebody took a door, a door from an apartment, and covered the lower part of a male corpse, the part where the legs and the lower stomach should be. Later, I passed behind the Posavina Hotel and saw parts of a child's legs. I reached the bridge. There were other people there. There were also police officers from the Brcko police station. There were also some of my acquaintances there. And maybe people began to talk there, to comment, who did it, what they did. All the police officers were lost. They didn't even know what to do there, should they secure the site or not. After about half an hour, a vehicle of the JNA appeared with about eight to ten people in the trailer. It was a pinzgauer, a larger one. All the men were armed in camouflage uniforms with helmets on their heads, and one of them jumped out from the vehicle and started to talk to one of the police officers, that they should clear the site and that there was some kind of commission coming there. Then the soldiers all got back into the vehicle and continued on their way to another part of the town of Brcko. I stayed there for about another half an hour. People continued to comment about what had happened. And then I went back to my apartment. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I inquire as to when we would break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was my intention to break after one hour and a half, so that would be in one or two minutes. If this would be a suitable moment, we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This would be convenient, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if first the witness would be escorted out of the courtroom. We have a break, Mr. Gasi. And then that I just for one minute put my schedules on the table so that you could respond to that. You're excused. We'll resume in 20 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind for the afternoon sessions, when we start at a quarter past 2.00, to have the first break at a quarter to 4.00, a 20-minute break. So we'd start at five minutes past 4.00, until 5.30, which would bring us another one hour and 25 minutes, then have another break of 20 minutes until 10 minutes to 6.00 and then continue from 10 minutes to 6.00 to 7.00. If this schedule would, either from the parties or from any of those assisting us just outside the courtroom, would -- if there would be any opposition to it, I'd like to hear that. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I requested if we could have one minute with you before we have the witness come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding Mr. Gasi, in preparation for his testimony today, we have been waiting clearance from a Rule 70 provider concerning two statements that he made some time ago, and our request has been outstanding since at least May of last year. Mr. Gasi testified in the Milosevic case in September of 2003. They also were waiting the same clearance from the same provider, but he was allowed to testify without that clearance. I understand from the Milosevic team that yesterday they received a written authorisation to provide those Rule 70 materials in that case, but that case only. I spoke with the representative from the provider in question, who advised me that it was the intention that the clearance would provide -- would cover this case and all other cases as well. However, because that was not put in writing, he requested that I not make the disclosure yet until he can either get it in writing or get an oral confirmation. I mentioned this to Mr. Stewart before we started today but I wanted to bring it to the Court's attention that we still have this. We have reviewed it and in our estimation it does not contain any strictly Rule 68 material, but it is in the nature of a Rule 66 statement, although not signed by the witness, it's more the report of an interview, but in our view it is in the nature of a Rule 66 statement, and we do want to provide it as soon as we receive clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If clearance has not been asked in respect of this case, then the only thing I could establish at this moment is that it would have been better to have asked it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We requested it in May, and then again when Milosevic was requesting the same, we asked that if we could be included in that same clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's good to be informed about it, but it doesn't change the present situation, as far as I understand. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Gasi back into the courtroom. I've got one question for you in between, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my witness summary, it's indicated that the estimated duration would be three hours, whereas I find in my most recent list four hours. Is there anything added to what was in the summary we received, that's the summary dated the 2nd of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the difference is, Your Honour, when we reduced our number of viva voce witnesses from a different number and we moved some people from one municipality to another, we made a decision to try and do more through him live because we had dropped some other witness to a 92 bis status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have expected then a summary adapted to that as well. But as it is now, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, when we broke, I think you had told us that after you had gone down to look at the damage at the bridge, you returned home. And what did you do when you got there? Did you make any arrangements with your family?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: When I returned home from the bridge, I found a neighbour in my apartment, a woman, who lives in the same building, in the apartment below ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: She is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did she give you any advice about what you should do?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: My wife had already talked to her. My wife, Jasminka asked me why do we have to leave Brcko. The lady said, "You see the war has already begun. You cannot stay here any longer. They will come from Bijeljina and they will transport you to Serbia. You'd better leave." [In English] I have a problem with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be a technical problem with the earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same. So it's not a matter of the headphones. I must say, I also hear some rumble on the earphones which might be the same, but stronger for the witness. Mr. Gasi, is it any better or is it still the same? It's still the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but there is some noise in my headphones that I hear at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have the same, and I notice that it depends on who speaks, what microphones are open. Is it better now? Yes. So it must have been one of your own microphones. But of course you can't -- it's not you to be blamed for it. If the matter has been solved, then please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at the screen. Did you have a chance to finish your last answer? You said your neighbour advised that you should leave. Was that the end of your answer?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Jasminka insisted, and kept on asking: "Why do we have to leave? Why should I leave? I don't understand."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But was there any further explanation from your Serb neighbour?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. She said: "Jasminka, war has started in Brcko. You would all be better off by leaving the town." I accepted that. I decided to accept her husband's offer to take us out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you travel with her husband and take your wife and child out of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. He drove my car. I sat next to him, and Jasminka was in the back. Before that, I called a friend of mine in Belgrade and arranged for him to meet us in Bijeljina. We heard that it would not be possible for us to cross the bridge on the Drina River, because the bridge was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have to travel through any checkpoints on your way from Brcko to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. From my apartment, on the road towards Elektrodistribucija, and on the road towards Bijeljina, the army had set up a mixed checkpoint, together with -- together with some people who wore camouflage uniforms. There were also people in camouflage uniforms who differed from the JNA uniforms. Those camouflage uniforms were blue, different shades of blue, and there were also two men from the Red Beret units. They checked our IDs. Actually, they checked his ID and then they concluded that he was a Serb and they told us that we were free to proceed, that we were free to pass that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "a mixed checkpoint," are you referring to the ethnicities of the people in the checkpoint or to the units that they were with?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I'm referring to different uniforms that I could see there. There were some people wearing olive-drab uniforms, some wore helmets on their heads. Two had red berets on their heads. And there were two more men in blue camouflage uniforms that I never saw before. And on their blue berets, there was a flag of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnicity of all these individuals was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. They didn't introduce themselves to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you manage to get to Bijeljina and make arrangements for your wife and child to join your friend and travel to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Bijeljina, and I met my friend a couple of hours later. He had come from Belgrade in his own car. He had had some problems at the Drina bridge. And I also met another friend from the kayak team of Yugoslavia. He also wore a soldier's uniform. And he told me not to go back to Brcko. I didn't listen to his advice. I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you return to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I probably believed that everything would be normal, as it was before. I still held my employment there, so that was probably another motive. I believe I had normal reasons to go back. It's very hard for me to explain why I went back, but I did. I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While you were in Bijeljina, did you notice anything about what military units, if any, were present in town?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were none in Bijeljina, but on the road from Brcko to Bijeljina, on the left side of the road, there were JNA vehicles parked. There were tanks. There were people-carriers, there were infantry vehicles. There were soldiers. They were just standing there. They were not moving, but they were all turned towards Brcko. This column was a couple of kilometres long, according to my estimate. In the town of Bijeljina, I didn't see any troops. There were police wearing blue uniforms. Some wore camouflage uniforms. We were not stopped. I didn't have any problems entering Bijeljina or returning to Brcko, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do when you returned to Brcko? Where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I stayed in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The day after the explosion at the bridge, were there any public announcements about what was happening in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 1st of May when the local Brcko TV aired a programme, and Mustafa Ramic, the president of the Municipal Assembly, appeared on the screen. And also I believe that Captain Petrovic, who introduced himself as somebody from the local barracks, the security officer. Mustafa Ramic said in his interview that they had agreed at the level of the municipality, with the people from the Brcko barracks, that the army would be given a mandate to take over the civilian life in town in the period of the next 48 hours, because some rumours had started circulating in town about paramilitaries from Serbia who had arrived in town. So the army accepted to control the civilian life in town. And that programme was then interrupted, and I don't know what happened next. Later on, Radio Brcko also repeated something along these same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple days after this broadcast, did you observe any fighting or any military activity in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Maybe on the 2nd or on the 3rd of May. I was in front of my building. It was around 10.00 in the morning. From the direction of south-east, two jet planes flew over Brcko. They were JNA jets. And they returned a couple of minutes later from the other direction. Again, they flew over the town. And all of a sudden we could hear powerful explosions coming from the direction where they had flown off to. Whether they bombarded or not, I don't know. I suppose so. I didn't see it. I only saw them when they were flying over Brcko and when they were returning from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the sound of explosions came from the direction in which you had seen them initially fly to and then return from?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what ethnic group lived in that part of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This is Mujkici local commune, and then Gluhakovac and then some Croat villages. I suppose that if not all, then 90 per cent of the people were Muslims and Croats. There were maybe some Serbs, but very few Serbs who lived on that stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a day when you were eventually arrested in Brcko? Do you recall what day that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I have repeated it many times: 27 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between the 1st of May, when you returned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Between the 30th April, when the bridge blew, and the 27th of May, when you were arrested, what were you doing in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I spent most of the time in my apartment. Several times I crossed the River Brka in order to visit my in-laws. And the last time I visited them was on the 3rd of May, in the morning. I returned to my apartment sometime around the 6th or the 7th of May, together with a neighbour of mine from my building, I went to the centre of the town. I went to the market -- where the marketplace used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is that area of town called?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is that area of town called, please?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Before the war, it was Brace Cuskica Street, across the road from the marketplace there was an arts and crafts centre that some people refer to as Stari Grad, the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen that morning at Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Shooting started. As we entered this area and came into the market area, all of a sudden shooting started behind our backs. I couldn't see what was going on, but there were bursts of fire. And the lady who was with me said we should hide. A woman whom she knew started calling to us from a nearby building and told us to come upstairs to her apartment. We did that. As we entered the apartment, I could see the Bimeks butcher shop below her window. The drapes were drawn, and as we were sitting in the apartment I could hear some more shots. I approached the window. I looked through the window. I pulled the curtains. And then I saw people being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. Would you tell us first: What was the first group of people you saw being executed? Where was that happening?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Across the road from that window where I was, there was a group --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my learned friend to be a little bit more careful because the witness said he saw people being executed and then Mr. Hannis said: "What was the first group of people you saw being executed?" The witness didn't refer to a number of different groups. He simply referred in very general terms to people being executed. So I'd invite my learned friend to be a little bit more careful not to lead the witness into that sort of area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your response, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hear my learned friend and I will try to take care in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do agree more or less to what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, could you tell us what was the first thing you saw with regard to people being executed? Where was that happening?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In front of the window where I was standing, across the road, on a plateau, behind the coffee bars and restaurants which were right in front of me. On my left-hand side, along the wall, a policeman wearing a blue uniform approached the people who were standing facing the wall of that building, and he shot in their heads, or in their backs. I can't remember. There were three such shootings, and I saw all three of them. I tried to describe all of them in detail in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were the three victims men or women? If you can tell.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I'm a hundred per cent sure about the three. They were all men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were they wearing? Civilian clothing or military?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you describe the policeman? Was there only one? And if so, what was he or she wearing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The policeman who shot in their backs, he wore a blue shirt with short sleeves, of the kind that police used to wear before the war. And he also had a pistol and blue trousers. And the others who were also shooting at people, they all war camouflage JNA uniforms with balaclavas, black balaclavas over their heads. One of them who may have been their commander shouted at them, and he would say: Thirty of them for one of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were the men in camouflage uniforms standing in relation to where you saw the policeman shooting the three people?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They were about 50 metres away from him, as the crow flies. They were in this area of this artisan centre, or the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were five to six in this first group, and then up at the plateau there were another four to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the first group of five or six, are you talking about the soldiers or victims?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The people who were getting killed were civilians, the victims; and the people who actually did the firing, they were wearing camouflage uniforms and had balaclavas on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you explain for the Court how many civilians were being shot by men in JNA uniforms with balaclavas, and how many soldiers there were in that group?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There were about ten, in two groups. And in those two groups, they killed about 10 to 12 people, plus those 3 men who were killed by this police officer in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we show the witness next exhibit, P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear that you have taken over more or less the numbering from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
