utterances.text: No. We received copies of the documents to be tendered, especially the photographs, with a, I would say, an exhibit number on it, attributed to that document by the Prosecution. And that's also what you mentioned. If you mention that number, we know exactly what exhibit we are dealing with. So that would be, I take it, then, that you'd like to show to the witness Exhibit 38078. Which would then, as the registrar will certainly confirm us, will be P3. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise what that's a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It's a part of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that depict the area in which the shootings you're describing occurred?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It depicts the building I was in. And this arts and crafts Stari Grad centre is across from that building I was in. And you can also see the SUP building. That's the new building. You can see it. It's painted white. You can see the roof. And then from that building, across from there, there's a little park and there's a hotel there. This is the SUP building, this is the park. This is the Hotel Posavina building. You just indicated it. Now if you go down a bit with the arrow, a bit lower, still lower, this is the building I was in. This is the place where these five or six people were executed. And then behind that, over those roofs, there's a plateau and another four to five people were executed there. If you take the arrow straight up -- a little bit lower. A little bit lower, to the right. Yes. Yes. A little bit up, please. A little bit up. And then again right, and lower, lower, all the way down. Yes. That building right there is where all three men were told to face the wall, and that's where they were shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By whom were those three men shot, again?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The police officer in the police uniform in the short-sleeved shirt, the blue police shirt and blue pants that he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the SUP building, what does SUP stand for?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Station, the station for the police. The Secretariat for Internal Affairs of Brcko, to be precise. If you take the arrow straight up, you will see the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, sir, is that the white building near the centre of the photograph, at the top?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What floor were you observing this from, the apartment of the friend of the woman that you were with?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you: Just below the building, or in the building, there's this Bimeks shop. So it's either on the first or the second floor. But in any case, it's just above this Bimeks shop, and there are no other floors except for that floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what the topography of the land is in that area; that is, is it flat or is there a slope in one direction or another?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: When you go from -- judging -- going by the picture, when you go from the Posavina Hotel, the whole road starts to slope downwards towards the Brka River. More or less, the place where I was was in the middle of this downward slope. Before the war, the street was called Brace Cuskic. I don't know what it's called now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from your position in that apartment, were you able to see over the buildings across the street to the location you described where the policeman was shooting three people?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, you can be sure that I did, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And likewise, the two groups of soldiers shooting people?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They were the closest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the victims that were being shot by the soldiers, how were they dressed? Were they in military clothing or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you see whether any of the victims had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we show the witness the -- well, may we have a number for the next exhibit, and this would be our number 38.105.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be Prosecution Exhibit number P4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise what that's a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. You can see a part of the Posavina Hotel, down there on the right side. And then if you look, you can see the road sloping downwards, as I explained. On the left side, you can see the beginning of these small shops which were in the arts and crafts centre in the Stari Grad, the cafes, little shops, small restaurants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that building is on the left side of the photograph, the big building there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Before the war, there was a casino there. I think it was called the Knutsen [phoen] Casino, in that building. Just in front of the casino was the building of the local HDZ, and also the Oslobodjenje cinema in that same building. So it was a little bit more to the left from this shop window that you can see in the photograph. There was also a hairdressing salon there, a small one. I think that perhaps this is the hairdressing salon. And then the entrance to the casino was just in front of it. And also, that's where the HDZ offices were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the shooting of three people by the policeman that you described earlier, can you tell us where that would have taken place on this photograph, if it's in this area?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. It was nearby. If we were now to go around the corner from the shop window, there is a path leading along a wall towards the Brka River, and that's where the incident took place, a little bit more when you go down there inside, on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next exhibit number for Photograph 38.106.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you tell the Court what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: You can see this street now that you asked me about just before, and you can see the exact place where this policeman killed those three people. I don't know whether they died on the spot, but in any case, I did see them fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is the Knutsen casino that you mentioned before shown on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: You can't see it right now because the image has shifted. Now we're looking at this road that leads between the building where the Knutsen casino was. This road, if you followed it all the way down, there is a cement wall, and there's -- at the end of it there is access which would take you down to the Brka River. But you can't see it. But that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may we show the witness the next photograph and give it the next number. This would be 38.084 in our numbering.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise what area this photograph is taken in?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. It was taken on the exact spot that we saw just before, but it's been probably taken from a different angle. But this is the same place that I was describing earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is the uniform that the man with the gun is wearing similar to the uniform you described the shooter wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Exactly the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may we show the witness the next exhibit, 38.086.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, again, is this the street that you described running next to the side of the Knutsen casino, where you saw the shooting of the three victims by someone in a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. You see the garbage container on it at the end of the street, and then behind the container there's a cement wall which separates the street from the Brka River. The Brka River is a bit lower down, so you can't see it, but that is that precise spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, one more in this series, 38.089.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we give it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Gasi, this is -- is this the -- sort of at the end of the street that you've described earlier, as running back toward the Brka River?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Not at the end and not in the middle of the street. It's sort of towards or near the middle of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where along the street were the three men shot when you saw this event on about May 7th?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This man on the right side who is shooting, from where he is standing, if you look, there is a window to the left with bars on it. That's where he made them face the wall, and that's where he shot them in the back, exactly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We don't need that one any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, what did you do after you saw these events occurring outside your friend's friend's apartment?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I was there until maybe 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening. Then the lady who was with me, from my building, managed to call a friend of hers, who came and collected the two of us from the apartment. We were not able to move around freely. She was afraid, because a curfew was imposed. I think it went into effect after 8.00. So nobody should have been on the streets of Brcko after 8.00. So I think her friend appeared a little bit before then, or perhaps at 8.00; I can't remember. But it was already beginning to get dark. And he brought us back to my building, and we didn't really leave the building any more, until the people from Elektro-Brcko came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far from the police station were these places where the executions took place? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: About 50 metres or 70 metres, to be more precise. It's about that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you still going to work any time between the 30th April and the time you were arrested on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you before: I was in the apartment until the 9th or the 10th of May. I can't remember exactly. Anyway, on that morning, the people from Elektro-Brcko came and they took me in their vehicles. So then from the 9th or the 10th of May, I was in Elektro-Brcko all the time, and I also worked around town. I moved around in the Elektrodistribucija vehicles, until they came and arrested me on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between the 9th or 10th and the 27th of May, were you also sleeping at your workplace at Elektro-Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I was sleeping and eating. I slept in the technical goods warehouse with the other electricians who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why were you doing that? Why were you sleeping at your workplace?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The director told us that this was a war labour assignment and you had to be there 24 hours. You had to be available. They had to know where you were at all times, for as long as these extraordinary measures were in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time before your arrest, did you, in the course of going out and working around town, did you see any dead bodies in Brcko town?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 1992, we left the Elektrodistribucija compound and started driving towards the town centre. Across the road from the Jelenka Vockic elementary school, there was a military police checkpoint. They stopped us. And as they explained to one of the Serb electricians who was driving us, they had to wait to receive permission to pass from somebody from the JNA garrison. That's what they told us. And then, after about half an hour or so, a vehicle appeared which used to drive the garrison commander around before the war, and in the vehicle was captain first class. I think he was in the reserves, but I know him as well. Captain Mitric, Slobodan Mitric. A soldier was driving him. When he turned up at the checkpoint, they talked to him. I saw that from the car. Then they came up to the Serb who was driving us and said that we can continue straight ahead towards the Galeb Hotel. And when we came near the Galeb Hotel, there is a parking space in front of the Galeb Hotel and the department store. We were supposed to turn left there and pass through the centre of town, but the man who was driving the car, he was -- on the right-hand side of this parking, there were garbage containers, and I could see parts of human bodies showing outside of these containers, legs and arms. And next to the containers there were three or four corpses lying there, in civilian clothes. In front of the Galeb Hotel, there were people sitting in olive-drab camouflage uniforms. They were sitting in front of the hotel on chairs which had probably been taken outside from the restaurant. So when we made the left turn, that's the image that stuck to my mind. After that, we went in the direction of the medical centre, in order to repair whatever we were supposed to repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gasi, can you tell the Court how big that garbage container was from which you saw body parts sticking out?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's where the containers are. Their volume is three, four, or a maximum of five cubic metres of garbage. And then there are these local vehicles, the sanitation company vehicles, which can pick up the container and tip the garbage into the vehicle that collects the garbage. I think to this very day you can find such containers around the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far away were the men in uniform from the garbage containers and the bodies that you saw.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: About 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may we have the next exhibit number for Photograph 38.059 and show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, is the area that you've been talking about shown in the photograph on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Here you can see the culture hall, and you can see the Partizan building, and also you can see one part of the Galeb Hotel. Here, where the arrow is now, this is not the parking. The parking is a bit lower, in front of the Galeb Hotel, but it is not depicted in this photo. This parking is in front of the culture home. If you were to move the arrow further down, there is another parking lot in front of the Galeb Hotel. But it is not depicted in the photo. Here you can see just one part of the Galeb Hotel, the Partizan sports hall, and the culture hall. This is the Partizan sports hall. If you move to the right now, that's the culture hall. This is the culture hall. You're showing it now. You are pointing at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the white building in the lower right corner of the photograph, what building is that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's the Galeb Hotel. I don't know what it's called now, but before the war it used to be Galeb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Partizan sports hall is the building just above that, as you're following along the street?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there. That is the building that you're now showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Gasi, during your work assignment between the 10th and 27th of May, do you recall an occasion when you were out working on top of a very tall pole and saw something unusual in a field near the Bimeks factory or farm?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It was not just a pole; it was a transformer pole which was about 20 metres high. On one occasion, we were supposed to replace the insulator tapes on those poles. And this is in the middle of the army shooting range. There is also a small stream close to that transformer pole that we were supposed to climb. And I was one of those who were selected to climb that transformer pole. I saw a white Bimeks TAM, lorry, which was parked in front of a hole. They were unloading human corpses and throwing them into that hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, first of all, what Bimeks was in Brcko at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Bimeks was a slaughterhouse, and also a processing plant for meat, for the slaughtered pigs and cows. They would also distribute all those meat products, not only in Brcko, but all over Bosnia and all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far away was this taking place from where you were on the pole? Approximately how far?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Between 100 and 150 metres, tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From that distance, were you able to tell what kind of clothing the bodies had?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They all wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you see what kind of clothing the men who were taking the bodies out of the truck and putting into the hole, what kind of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms that belonged to the JNA. They were olive-drab camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many men were taking the bodies out?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I saw two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were there any other people around besides the two men unloading the truck?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other vehicles or equipment around the hole?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There was a construction machine, a bulldozer, as they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I would like to have the next photograph given a number, please. It's our 38.081.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you recognise the area where that photograph is taken of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. I know exactly where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges where that is?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As you're walking from Elektrodistribucija, and when you go toward Bijeljina, there is a gas station called Mistrafovici there. Instead of going right, you turn right [as interpreted] towards the pig and the cattle farm. And as you drive along some 300 metres further on, there's a fence, which fenced off a company that was supposed to move from that area. And this was all within the compound of the JNA shooting range. Now, this place that we are looking at is immediately behind that fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this hole in the location that you've described seen from the pole, or is this a different location?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This is not that place. That place was some hundred metres away from the place depicted in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how you're able to tell the difference?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I already saw these photos, and if you look to the left from this excavator you can see a lamp and a fence, and the only place you could find this type of fence and this type of lamppost was Brcko, and that's how I recognised that this was the JNA shooting range, because this is the only place where you can -- you could find this type of fence and this type of lamppost and lamp. I already saw this photo somewhat enlarged. I don't know whether it was during my interview when I gave the statement, or maybe here. In any case, I saw this photo a bit enlarged, maybe from a different angle, so I could see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in this photo, are you able to see a part of the Bimeks truck that you're describing, or one that looks like the truck you were describing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: This is the same type of truck. In the right-hand side corner, a white TAM, which bore the inscription "Bimeks" on it. That's exactly the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I ask you one thing? Could you please invite the witness to perhaps a part of the photograph that was just enlarged, where the lamppost was, to indicate where he sees the fence. Because I have some difficulties in following.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll enlarge that part of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll try and do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, did you hear that, and can you indicate where the fence is in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. If you look closer at this photo, you will see a fence. It is a bit overgrown, but there is a fence. You can see it. And maybe at a distance of 100 or 200 metres, at every 100 or 200 metres, there is one lamp. It was my company that installed these lamps. Now you are showing the fence. This is the fence that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what kind of fence that is? Is it a wood fence? Is it a wire fence?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It was a metal fence which was made to order. I believe that there is a concrete base on which this metal fence was mounted and put together. And every 100 or 200 metres there is a lamp. These lamps are integral parts of this fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a hard copy. I don't know if that is easier to see from than on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar was so kind to provide the hard copy, and we have looked at it, and there would be no need just -- if we want to look at a hard copy, we'll ask the registrar. That will save us copying again three times in colour the original exhibit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And may the next exhibit be given the next number, please, and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P10, Prosecution reference 38.082.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would that be 11?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P11. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you see this photograph? And tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It's the same place. Everything is the same. Maybe the angle is different; however, the place is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see the fence better in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I could see it well in the previous one, but you can also see it in this photo. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we can take that away, and I want to move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you've told us before you were arrested on the 27th of May, 1992. Can you tell us where that happened and who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, in the morning, around 9.00 in the morning, a red van stopped in front of the Elektrodistribucija gate. Two police officers came out of the van. I knew both of them. They wore police uniforms. One of them was Dragan Pantelic, the other one was Radivoje Knezevic. They entered the area where the director slept and then they approached me. They called me by my name and then they told me that I was to go with them. The director asked them where they were taking me. They answered: This is none of your business. If anybody asks, just tell them that the police had taken him away. Then they pushed me into the back part of the van. They drove me to the town, to the police station, to the so-called SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the next --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. May the witness be shown the next exhibit number. It would be our 38.095.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you tell the Court what is in photograph P12.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's the SUP, the police station in Brcko. It is the entrance. What you are showing, all of it, that's the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long were you kept at the police station after you were taken there by those two men you named?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They pushed me into a room on the right-hand side. There was no light. They just shoved me into that room. Later on I saw that there were already two people in there, and I stayed there for maybe 40 minutes or an hour. They didn't beat me. Nobody did anything to me. And later on, they came to fetch me and they took me out of that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know the other two people that were in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I knew them well. I didn't recognise them at first, but I did know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Without naming them, can you tell us their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: One of them was a Muslim, and the other one was a mixed Serb who was a bit of a local problem. He was a petty thief, a petty criminal. They were both in that room. I had a quick chat with the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were you taken when you were removed from the room, and who took you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: A local Serb whom I knew, wearing a JNA uniform without a hat on his head, he came. He knocked on the door and he said: "Gasi come with me." His name was Pera. That's what we called him. He held my ID card in his hand. There was another man with him. He wore a camouflage uniform. Judging by his accent, he was a Serb. And this guy says: "Shall we tie him?" And the former one said: "No. He's a good man. Don't do that." Then I was put into a pick-up, and as we were leaving the SUP building, I asked Pera: "Pera, what are you doing, and where are you taking me?" And he said: "We're taking you to Luka, to the harbour." And that's where they took me. This Pera, he had an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know Pera's last name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Maybe Bozic or something like that. I can't remember exactly. But I know the guy. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the next exhibit, and may it be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the next exhibit and may it be given the next number in order, our 38.093.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you tell us what this building is?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's the Posavina Hotel building. And you can also see the corner of the old municipality building. And this passage leads towards the summer hall of the Radnik cinema. In any case, this is the Posavina Hotel building in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where is that located in relation to the police station? How far?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Fifty to seventy metres, according to my estimate. It may even be a hundred. It really depends on the angle from which you are looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next number in order, for Photograph 38.072.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you tell the Court what that is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: These are hangars, the hangars of the Brcko harbour on the Sava River. Yes. These are the hangars. You're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the name of this area?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Brcko had a harbour, Luka. Luka was the name of this area, which means "harbour."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next number in order for 38.083.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance to the Luka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at Luka after you were taken there on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Until the 7th of July, 1992, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next number in sequence for 38.090.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please tell us, Mr. Gasi, what that's a picture of.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: You are showing the hangars where I was. The first hangar was empty when I arrived. I was a bit more to the right, in the second hangar. Now, the first one that you showed just a little while ago was totally empty. But I was in both of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were you first taken when you arrived at Luka?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Across the road from these hangars there's a building, a prefabricated house which housed the offices for the admin. workers who used to work in Luka before the war. A policeman from the Brcko police station took me there, and this guy whose name was Pudic was waiting for me there. He hit me with a pistol on the head, and they took me into the first office on the right-hand side. As I entered the office, there were four people there, plus Pudic, who was behind my back. He pushed me in. I said: "Good morning." And one guy with a beard jumped to his feet. And he was holding something like that fireman's hose. And he jumped on his feet, wanted to hit me with that hose. But then he changed his mind, and he says: "Can you greet me in the Serbian way?" And then I said: "Yes, I can." And I answered: "God help you, brothers." And then he said: "And same to you. Fuck you." And then I sat on the bench, and one of them asked me: "Where were you in 1982?" I didn't know why they were asking me that. On my left-hand side in that same office where they were, there was a guy sitting. He was a friend of mine from the kayak club. He was a JNA officer. He was an active-duty military man. He served in Split. He also wore a uniform. He turned towards me and he told the others: "Don't mistreat this man. I know him well. He is a native of Brcko. He's a very well-known Yugoslav athlete." When he told them that, then the others calmed down and one of them said to Pudic: "Pudic, take him to the first hangar and don't touch him there." Then Pudic took me out of there. We entered the first hangar that you see in front of you. It was empty. And as he put me in the hangar, behind the door there was a chair and he told me: "Sit on the chair and don't move." I sat in that chair, I waited, and some 40 minutes later Pudic appeared again and told me: "Okay. Go to the other part of that hangar." These hangars have a partition, a high metal partition with a door. The door was open and I entered the second part of the hangar. On both sides of the hangar there were people lying on the concrete floor. There were some people lying on cardboard. In any case, on both sides of the hangar there were people prostrated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Gasi. You mentioned Pudic, who hit you when you first arrived at the office. Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know that his name was Pudic. And before the war, he was on the police force. And it seems to me that he is still a member of that same police station. If I were to give you any names, I may be wrong, but I know the man very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he wearing any uniform on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform. He didn't wear a JNA uniform. He wore a blue police uniform, like the ones that they used to wear before the war. That's the kind of uniform that he wore at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of the JNA officer that was in the office?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I can, but if the Trial Chamber agrees, I'd rather not mention his name. If the Trial Chamber insists, I can give you his name. I'd rather not. I know the man very well. I know his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how important it is for the Prosecution case to hear that name. If so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go in private session just for the name, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Mr. Gasi, we'll have a break for another 20 minutes. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, during the break, some attention was paid to the quality of the sound. If there's any further problem, please indicate so. We might not be able to make it perfect, but if it's -- please be aware of it's of our concern. And for the parties, I would like to indicate to you that the last five minutes of today's hearing, I'd like to spend some time on some procedural issues, smaller ones. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we give the next exhibit, P17, if that's the next number, for 38.092.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you tell us what photograph is on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Now you can see, this building on the right, that's where the offices are where I went for interrogations, and across from them is the hangar where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the office where you were first taken when you arrived at Luka, is that shown in the picture?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that. You can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... On the photo? Which side?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Here you can see, on this picture on the right, two windows, a little bit to the left, and then up a little bit, if you pass, you can see an entrance. On the right side there is the door. So that's the first part of the office. And then if you continue along straight, I think that there are two more entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned when you were first taken to the office, you mentioned Pudic, who hit you, and the JNA officer. Who were the other people in the office when you got there, and were they wearing any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In the office, on the right, there are two men inside. They were sitting on chairs. They were in camouflage uniforms. One of them had a beard, and he had a large Kokarda insignia on the left. It was a metal Kokarda insignia which he wore. When I entered the office, there were two more men sitting inside. One of them was facing me directly. He was a younger person. He was a lieutenant. He wasn't wearing a camouflage uniform, but an olive-drab uniform. The other man was also wearing an olive-drab uniform. And then, as I said, there was also that captain who I knew personally. He was sitting to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us, please, what the Kokarda is, what that looks like and what that's associated with, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's the insignia. I know this. I learnt this also in history classes. It's insignia which the Serbian Chetniks wore during the First and the Second World Wars. This insignia was worn later by people who belonged to the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break I think you told us you were initially placed in the first hangar and then later on moved over into the second hangar, where there were several other people. Can you tell us how many people were in the second hangar?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That first day when I arrived, there were approximately, approximately, 200 people. Throughout my entire time in the hangar, for those 10 or 11 days that I spent there, I counted them to myself. So sometimes I would count 100, 120, sometimes 170 men, then sometimes a group would leave. They would go to work somewhere. Then they wouldn't come back. Others would come, five or six new people would be brought during the day. So I would add those people up. So all the time it was from 100, 120, 150, 170, sometimes up to 200 people were there at certain times. Sometimes I counted them and sometimes I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you tell the Court, please, what the conditions were like in the hangar where you were kept with these other people.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All those people were lying on cardboard boxes. Some were lying on the concrete, some just lay on their own clothes. I lay on cardboard boxes. Mostly people were either sitting down or lying down when I entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how big was that hangar that you were in with these other people, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know. I walked its width and length many times. So perhaps it was 35 to 40 metres wide and about 70 metres long. I used to walk down both hangars, because they were separated by doors. So I walked everywhere. So it was about from 35 to 40 metres wide, and then 50 metres long. So that's about the size of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tell us about the people that were kept in there with you. Were they men, women, children?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All of them were men. There was only one woman, and her son was with her. She was a retarded woman from Brcko. I knew her from before the war. When I came to the hangar, she was there as well, on the 27th of May. I think that two days afterwards she was released, together with her son. I don't know where she was taken. I don't know if she survived or not. I'm not able to tell you that. But I do know that while I was in the hangar, she was there for a day or two, and that was the only woman I saw in the hangar then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see other women at the hangar -- I mean at Luka, but not in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: One of them used to come from the building where the offices were. She would come in very often, accompanied by the soldiers. She would enter the hangar. I don't know why she did that. Once they brought her in to see if she knew anybody. But I knew her also. I'd seen her around before. And even later, I had a chance to speak to her. She said that she slept in these offices, the offices were closed. There were about five or six other women that she mentioned were with her. On another occasion, another woman came into the hangar together with Kole, Kosta Simeunovic and Goran Jelisic. That was that Monika, she was with him at the time. I think she appeared at the hangar twice with him during the entire time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first woman you mentioned, not Monika, what was the ethnicity of that woman?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I know her very well because her former husband was also a rower at one of our clubs. So I knew her. Her name was Ruzica. I think she was an ethnic Croat, and I believe that she lived in Gunja, across the Sava River bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the men who were kept in the hangar with you, do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: At the time I was there, I think that 90 per cent of all the people were Muslims. There were also several Croats, and there were also us Siptar, as they call us, of Albanian origin. It doesn't matter that I wasn't born there, but I belonged to that group of Siptars. And there were also three or four people of Kosovar origin, just like myself. So most of the people there were Muslims, there were some Croats and also some Albanians or Siptar, as they call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is Siptar a derogative term for Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's the way they used it. However, in the Albanian language, Albania is called Shqiptrie, so that's where that comes from. So probably they turned this historical term into a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the men that were kept there, were they -- were any of them soldiers or uniformed personnel that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All the people that I saw in Luka at the time were in civilian clothes. There were a couple of men in pajamas as well. I don't know how they ended up wearing pajamas, but anyway, there were some men in pajamas there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know many of these people, or any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: All of them, or nearly all of them, were from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the age range of the men kept in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The woman, who was the only woman there when I got there, and her son, I think he was maybe between 15 and 17 years old. There was another young man, together with his father, who was there. He was maybe about 15. The rest of the men ranged from about 20 up to even 70 or 75 years of age. The elderly ones, perhaps there were four or five of them, and the rest were mostly people in their 40s, 50s, in their 30s, 25 years old, or 20. That was the age range.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the time that you were there from the time of your arrest, how many days total?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, if I'm not mistaken, I think I was there for 10 or 11 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the day on which you were released?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember it very well. It was the 7th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time, were you and the other men in the hangar allowed to leave and go about freely?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I cannot hear the translation right now, but I did understand your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Turn the microphone on, Mr. Prosecutor, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you or any of the other men allowed to leave the hangar and move about freely while you were at Luka?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you locked in the hangars?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: We were in the hangar, and only the first hangar had its door open, the metal door. It was about 50 to 70 centimetres open. If you wanted to go out for air. But those of us who were in the second hangar, if we wanted to go out and get some air, we had to go to the first hangar and then squeeze through the gap. Outside the door there was a man, a soldier, in a reserve JNA uniform. So each time we went out, we had to ask him if we could go to the latrine or to have a drink of water, and then they would let us go for two or three minutes. And they would always check to see how long we would stay in the bathroom or in the latrine, just opposite from the hangar where we were. There were two bathrooms and two latrines there. And all of that was there. We slept there, we ate there, we drank there. Everything was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was the soldier armed who was watching you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. They were always armed. All of them had weapons, either automatic or semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know any of these men in JNA uniforms with weapons? Were they local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Some of them were. And we managed to get in touch or to establish contact with most of them. They would come into the hangar and we would chat. I knew some of them. Some of them were our local Serbs from Brcko. Sometimes, when there was a change of shift, sometimes they would come from Bijeljina or from the villages around Bijeljina. Sometimes, if they were friendly, we would manage to establish some kind of contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to the JNA uniformed men who were guarding you, were there any other uniformed men who came into the camp during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. People came in camouflage uniforms, different -- members of their different armies would come. There were people who came from the republican SUP of Serbia. People came in camouflage uniforms, wearing the insignia of Arkan's group. Ranko Cesic would come in wearing a JNA camouflage uniform. Goran Jelisic would come in. One evening, about five or six of them came in. It was after midnight. Perhaps it was 2.00 a.m. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and they had flashlights. They started to beat us, kick us, said that we should get up. We had to sing Serbian songs, and they said: "Sing them loudly, as loudly as you can." And this went on for perhaps 40 minutes. "Sing louder, louder." And they were hitting us as we were doing this. You couldn't see who they were because they were pointing the flashlights into our faces. I was lucky. I didn't get beaten too much. I did sing, though. So there were people coming in wearing different uniforms. There were different people. But all of them wore the olive-drab-coloured uniforms. They were either of a darker or lighter shades. There were people in old JNA uniforms, new JNA uniforms. All of them put in an appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have an understanding during the time you were there of who was in charge of Luka camp? Was there one individual that fit that description?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The second day, Kosta, Kole, Simeunovic, a local Serb in a police uniform, a blue police uniform, came to the hangar. He introduced himself to us new people who arrived. And the other men who were already there told us about it. He said: "I'm Kosta, Kole, most of you know me from Brcko. I am the commander of the Luka Brcko camp. When you are interrogated, I would be present." And then he told us what we were supposed to do during the day. This happened on the second day of my stay in Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think earlier you mentioned another female who was in the camp named Monika. Who was Monika?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That was his stepsister, Kosta's stepsister, Monika.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what ethnicity were Monika and Kole?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I cannot say about Kosta. He's probably a Serb. His father's a Serb. His mother is maybe a Croat. I don't know. Maybe she is a Croat or a Serb. And as for Monika, I don't know exactly. I don't know who her father is or how she declared herself. But anyway, she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was her role at the camp? What did she do at Luka?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: As I told you before, I think she appeared there on a couple of occasions. Both times she was in Goran's company. She was wearing civilian clothes. I don't know. She was wearing a skirt, summer skirt, short summer skirt. She wasn't in uniform. She appeared with him. One time when she came with him, he was angry, he was shouting and waving his gun around the camp and she went across to the other side. There was a young man there. Admir Didic was his name. They brought him. He was wearing his pajamas. He was already beaten up and bloodied. She went up to him, I guess he looked at her and she said: "Are you thirsty?" I don't know whether he said that he was or wasn't. I couldn't hear his answer. But anyway, she started to pour a Coca-Cola over his head from a large bottle, a bottle that can hold a litre and a half. And when she poured that over his head, then she hit him on the head with the bottle. The bottle shattered and then he fell down. I don't know. Then Goran had his own show: "I killed 98 people. Fuck you balijas. I will kill 98 more of you." And then Kosta came and tried to calm down the situation. And in the meantime he was walking around and kicking people and waving his gun around. And then all three of them went out. That was that one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. You're talking about Goran. What was his last name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Serb. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what -- was he in uniform? Did he belong to a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That time when he came to the hangar, he wore a camouflage uniform of the JNA. I didn't see any other insignia on it. He didn't wear a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of camouflage uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: From the uniforms that I know, I think that was the camouflage uniform of the JNA. I don't know any other ones. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname that was known to the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. They called him "Adolf," and he himself, that time when he came to the hangar, said, he said "Goran Jelisic, Adolf." And the first time when I met him. I didn't meet him, but the first time that he appeared in the hangar he said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you testified just a few minutes ago that he said he had killed 98 and he would kill 98 more. Did the prisoners that you talked to mention or tell you that he had killed other people before you arrived in Luka?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, it was very dangerous to speak of such things amongst us prisoners in Luka at that time. But yes, two men -- actually, three men from Elektrodistribucija, a father and son from Elektrodistribucija, and another one of my colleagues from work, who also did the same kind of jobs as I did, told me that he was present. I don't know when. Goran committed some murders in Luka. So this is what I heard from those three people who were there. However, nobody dared to say anything more than that in Luka, and all the things that were said, we had to wait for darkness to fall so that the neighbour who was lying down next to you wouldn't see you, for whatever reason. Everything that was discussed that went on in the hangar was always talked about in whispers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you that the next photograph, 38.101, be given the next exhibit number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you have that photograph on the screen before you, and can you tell us what that's a picture of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I know very well where this is. You can see the manhole. It's just across from the hangar where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "manhole," can you tell us where in the picture you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. You are just pointing to it with the arrow. That's the manhole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's in the lower left-hand corner of the picture, what looks like some sort of grating, I would call?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's a receptacle for sewage, for waste water, for rainwater. Near that place -- I mean, if you go straight down to the Sava River, there's a large pipe which actually links up the whole waterworks and sewage system in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And had some of the other detainees in the hangar with you told you that there was anything special about that grate?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I will tell you the name. Smajo Delic told me at the time that he was present when Jelisic lined up three or four men near that manhole and stepped on their heads and fired into their heads. He said that he himself had survived this execution. How, I don't know. And these two other men, father and son, Abid and Osman Stranjac were also in Luka. Osman told me that from that place where the arrow is right now, at that place - and this is what he said, I am telling you what I heard - that almost 80 people were killed, and from that place they were loaded up into a JNA TAM 5000-D truck. He helped to load up those dead bodies. I don't know where they were taken. He didn't tell me that. But anyway, he said that he had counted 80 people who were killed that day. That's what I heard. I don't know if that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Gasi: Did you personally see anyone killed during the time that you were at Luka?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell the Judges about when that occurred and how that occurred.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: If we move from this place to the right, if you move the arrow to the right, the office is on the right-hand side from this manhole. On one occasion, the hangar was closed. On that day, we couldn't go out. Everything was calm. And all of a sudden we heard a noise coming from the outside. As I was sitting in the hangar, I could hear people shouting, and shouting: "Come on. Move. Outside." As I was by the door, I looked in that direction, and from the office where I had once being interrogated, four civilians came out. Ranko Cesic followed them and shot them in the back. Two of them fell on the ground. Whether he killed them on the spot, I don't know. In any case, I heard five or six shots all together. I also saw another local Serb from Brcko who was standing, leaning on the wall next to the office. He was observing the whole scene. His name is Miso Cajevic. He entered the hangar twice while I was there. Both of them wore camouflage uniforms at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with those two men when this shooting occurred?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: There was another person in police uniform. I believe that it was Pudic. Whether they shot or not, I don't know. I only saw Ranko shooting them in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to indicate: This is an incident which Mr. Cesic has pled guilty before you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we have the next exhibit photo 38.108 given the next number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise who that's a photo of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know who this is. It's Ranko Cesic, a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he live in your building?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, he did. We lived in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the next photograph, 39.109, given the next number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I do. Goran Jelisic, Adolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I draw your attention to the fact that if you say I want to ask you about Mr. Jelisic, then ask for the next photograph and ask the witness who is on this photograph, that might not assist the Chamber in the most perfect way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, was there also a soldier there or an officer in the camp named Major Vojkan?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He also came twice or three times. Major Vojkan Djukanovic, he wore a camouflage uniform of the JNA, and he also bore the rank of a JNA major. He introduced himself to us. He delivered a few speeches as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was his role at the camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: According to him, according to what he told us on the first time as he entered the hangar, he asked us to approach him because he wanted to tell us something. On that occasion, he told us that he was the commander of the Luka camp and that he would try to save as many people as possible. And then he asked some people whom he had saved before I came, and he told them: "You know, don't you, that I saved you when you were being interrogated?" And then he said: "Well, see, men, the times are different. We are going to organise ourselves better. You're going to be safer here from now on. The situation in Luka is now improved. It's not what it used to be." And then he invited some other people whose names he even remembered, to vouch for that. And after all of these words that he told us, a group came into the hangar. They brought us cookies, cubes of sugar, probably cigarettes as well. They would throw all that amongst the detainees. On that same day, those who had come with sugarcubes and cigarettes and cookies, who managed to catch them, the people who had brought all these things in the first place took these people out and then they beat them. So when they came back into the hangar, they were all black and blue from beating. And that's what happened almost every day in the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion where one of the detainees was abused by a person who described himself as a Chetnik from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. There was Ibrahim Levic, who slept next to me on a cardboard, just like me. Somebody who introduced himself as Enver, as a Chetnik, stormed in. He had a knife and told this guy: "Stand up." He grabbed him by the neck and he carved a cross on his forehead. And then he also kicked him. And this man fell to the ground. He was bleeding. That's what Enver did on that occasion when he entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the shooting by Ranko Cesic during your time at Luka. Did you see dead bodies outside the hangars?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: On one occasion we were taken out of the hangar. There were four or five of us. We were supposed to do something. And they took us between the hangars, there is a passage between the hangars. Three men came. One wore a camouflage uniform, and the two others were guards, wearing uniforms of the JNA reserve. Behind the hangar there are two railroad tracks. There were some railway carriages there. And as we were taken to an open area covered with gravels, they told us to go a bit to the left, towards the Sava River, to a group of bodies that were down on the gravel. They stayed behind us. And one of them told us: "Grab them by their legs and by their arms and throw them into the river." We started doing that. I believe that I myself and another neighbour of mine managed to throw four bodies into the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about these bodies. Approximately how many were there at this location?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but I believe there were between 15 and 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they men, women, children?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I can't be sure whether they were women or not, but I'm sure that there were no children. I would have recognised children's bodies. I'm sure that there were men. The four bodies that I threw into the river were men. There may have also been women on the pile, but I'm not sure. I am sure, however, that there were no children's bodies in that pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of clothing were they dressed in?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't see a single uniform. They were all clothed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you see any injuries on their bodies?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. There were some bloodstains on their backs, and holes -- and on two bodies I saw holes on the necks, and on one body I saw that an ear was missing, and that was the first guy that I threw into the river. I believe -- as far as I can remember, one of them opened his eyes. I don't know whether he was alive or not. In any case, his eyes were open. We threw him into the river as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these holes you described, are you able to give us any better description of what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: We could see bloodstains on those -- on the clothes of those bodies. On one of them I could see that the right part of the head was badly injured. One part of the ear was missing. Most of these bodies I believe had been shot, either in the back or in the head. The ones that I had an opportunity to look at better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of the ones you were able to look at, were you able to recognise anyone either by facial features or clothing or anything else?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I believe I recognised a young man from my club. He had a sports T-shirt on. He was also shot in the back, close to his shoulders. His yellow T-shirt was bloodstained. He wore a pair of jeans and trainers. I didn't turn him around because I was not the one who carried him into the river. But as I was looking at him on that pile, from the back, I thought that I had recognised him. There was also another man from my company, and I believe that I also recognised him by the shoes and by the clothes that he was wearing. I believe I recognised the leather jacket he always wore as he came to work. And I believe that I recognised him as well. I cannot be a hundred per cent sure that they were the people that I thought they were, but in any case, I think that I did recognise the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of those two people that you thought you might have recognised?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may, could I return to Exhibit P14, which was shown to the witness earlier? If we could put that on the screen before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you now? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The electronic version is not on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We showed you that picture earlier. Can you tell us, from that picture, where you came out of the hangar and where you went to throw bodies in the river?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: If you point your arrow to the first hangar from which we came. This is the door through which we came out. Now move the arrow up, up, parallel with the building of the Luka. Yes. That's the way to go. Here, at the end of this set of hangars, there is a passage, and I believe that you can see the railway carriages in the photo if you move the arrow through the passage. Here, this is where the two rows of railway carriages were. I can still see them. And approximately where the arrow is. And if you move to the left, downwards, there was some gravel. Here there is a path down there. Here, exactly. You're okay here. The bodies were somewhere around here. We had to go down to the bank. This area was all open plain. It was not so overgrown. It was plain open area. You could see the bank across the river in Croatia. We came close to the river. We threw bodies into the river. As we threw one, we would go back to the pile, took another one and threw him into the river as well. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to throw all the bodies into the river or did something stop you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't, because they started shooting from the Croatian side. I don't know whether they were shooting at us. We could hear bullets hitting the railway carriages. People started running towards the railway carriages. The soldiers had already hid behind them. Somebody started shouting at us: "Motherfuckers, we're going to kill you all." And they started cocking their rifles. Then another soldier said to the first one: "Stop talking bullshit. Leave people alone." And then we returned to the hangar, and then this soldier told us: "You'd better keep quiet about what you had done and what you had seen."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then did you return to the hangar after that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us how the first day you arrived you were hit on the head by Mr. Pudic. Were you yourself personally physically abused during your 10 or 11 days at Luka, besides that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He didn't hit me in the head. Actually, he missed my head and hit me in the ear. But on that same day, I was beaten up. That was a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tell the Judges, please, how that happened and who did that to you.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. When I was allowed to go to that second hangar, maybe an hour or two hours later, a person appeared wearing a camouflage uniform with the Arkan's soldiers' insignia on his arm. His name was Zivan. He had long hair tied into a ponytail. He entered and came up to the middle of the hangar. There were two other men following him, wearing a JNA reserve army uniforms. He was the only one wearing a camouflage uniform. He said: "Where is that Siptar who arrived earlier today?" I got up. Then he said: "Come closer." As I was approaching him, he held his arm behind his back, and as I was some metre away from him, he said: "Come on. Come closer." I came closer, and then he waved his right arm. He had a key in his hand, a key which weighed about two kilos, approximately. And he hit me in the right shoulder. Then he wanted to hit me in the head, but missed. Then he tried to hit me in the head again. He missed and he hit me in the other shoulder, somewhere in the neck area. When he hit me the second time, I fell on the concrete floor. And I heard one of them saying: "This guy looks really strong. You have to hit him twice to throw him on the ground." I received a few more kicks in the head and in the stomach area, in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you suffer any long-term consequences as a result of that beating?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No. The only thing I suffered was the buzzing sound in the head, and I also had a pain in the upper part of my head. When I arrived in a refugee centre, later on in my life, they did some x-rays in order to see whether something was broken, but nothing was broken. I did suffer pain, but now I can hear all right and I can see all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the item he hit you with is described as a key. Can you describe for us what that looked like and what it's used for?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It was similar to a monkey wrench that is used for tightening firemen's hoses one to another. This is what firemen used when they were mounting their hose together. They used this thing in the shape of a letter "C." It was a metal object similar to a monkey wrench. It was a piece of tool that firemen use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gasi, during your time at Luka, were you taken to the office to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: On the following day, in the morning, Kosta came, and from the hangar, I went to the office, on the left-hand side. As I entered the office, a police inspector was there, Petar Kaurinovic, also known as Pero. Zoran Kondic was with him. He used to be a crime technician in the Brcko police before the war. And there was an acquaintance of mine, Petar Zaric, who belonged to the reserve police unit, together with the two of them. They didn't beat me. I sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to Kosta and these policemen you've described, was there anyone else that sat in during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Only the three of them were in that office, in the room where I was. There was also another office. I could see them through the open door. But these people were not present while I was being interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did they ask you about?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Since the three of them knew me from before, Petar told me: "Before we start, Isak, I can tell you that your father and your brothers and your nephew were also here. I made sure that they are all right. Now they are at home, and you don't have to worry about them."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did they ask you about after they told you that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The first question was: "Isak, do you have any weapons?" That's what Petar asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I said I didn't have any. And then he said: "But you had a licence to carry a pistol." I said: "Yes, but people from the barracks came and took it away from me and gave me a receipt." And then he says: "Ah, this is really good that you have this receipt. It may be a lifesaver for you in the future."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they ask you anything about other Muslims in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me whether I knew any Muslim extremists from the SDA, the Green Berets. I said: "Pero, I don't know any Muslim extremists. All I know, and people I know are the people who were with me in the SDA. And if there is anything else I can assist you with, I will gladly do that. You just keep on asking and I'll try and answer." At the end, he asked me whether I voted for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina in the referendum. I said: "Yes, I did." And he says: "Well, that's the biggest mistake in your life." And then I said: "Pero, if that is the biggest mistake, then kill me. I did vote, and that's how things are." And then he told me: "No. No. We are not going to kill you. We don't kill people. I'm not here to kill you." And this and that. And then he asked me whether I had been ill-treated. I said: "No, I wasn't." And then he said: "Why do you have bruises all over your head?" And I said: "Well, these are bruises from sleeping on the concrete floor." And then he says: "Just tell me if anybody ill-treated you. We know you. We know who you are. We are going to help you." And then I said: "Well, if you're going to then help me, then help me leave this place. I don't know to be here, if possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why did you tell them that you had not been beaten, even though that was the cause of your injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it's better to keep your mouth shut, because after the interrogation, I had to go to the hangar again, and I really didn't know who would come after Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before you returned to the hangar after that interrogation, did you have occasion to talk with anyone else in the office area?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Not at that occasion. When they told me I was free to go, he said that he would see what he could do so that I don't spend too long there. I went out and I returned to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who told you that he would see what he could do?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Petar said that as I was leaving that room where they were, that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a time shortly after that interrogation that you spoke with a JNA lieutenant near the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Once when they allowed me to go to the toilet, to that bathroom, when I went into the bathroom, when the guard allowed me to go, the guard in front of the hangar, I then suddenly heard that somebody had come in after me. I stayed a little longer inside, and then when I came out, I saw that lieutenant whom I saw on the first day when I came to the Luka. From the first moment I saw him, when I saw his eyes, he seemed to me to be a good person. And he told me, in the corridor: "For God's sake, man. I listened to your interrogation. I heard where your wife is. Do you want me to call her? Do you have the phone number in Belgrade where she is?" I said: "Yes, I will give it to you." And I did give it to him.
